person.name: Contributor 01
person.overview:
I traced requests through three handoffs and chose to add next-owner and return-date fields to the existing shared form instead of introducing a new application, because volunteers used a shared computer and another login would add a step. The shared-computer constraint is my contemporaneous report; this does not establish that it was the only possible design.

The experience changed the question I asked: instead of treating every missed handoff as something I should personally chase, I began asking whether ownership and escalation were clear enough for someone else to act, while still helping with exceptions. This is my personal reflection, not a measure of team performance or a claim about a lifelong trait.

accounts.title: Atlas / North Desk trial
accounts.summary:
I took on handoff investigation, intake-form implementation and defect follow-up for a trial approved for one library desk team; Contributor 02 retained equipment policy and approval. The January proposal and February brief establish remit and approval, not deployment.

By April, the original desk team was still using the form and escalation note; Contributor 04 and the coordinator continued to run review and answer exceptions, while my return-date correction remained in place. Continued use was reported for the original team only, and volunteers still needed help with exceptions.
accounts.context:
The follow-up did not measure time saved and did not establish independent operation. The easier-to-follow instructions were qualitative feedback, not a time or autonomy measure.

A second-desk trial was deferred because supervised shifts could not be staffed, while the current desk could continue; whether the form would work at another desk remained unknown. The deferral reflects staffing, not a demonstrated failure of the form.
accounts.aim: I took on handoff investigation, intake-form implementation and defect follow-up for a trial approved for one library desk team; Contributor 02 retained equipment policy and approval. The January proposal and February brief establish remit and approval, not deployment.
accounts.contribution:
I implemented separate owner and approver fields, return-date validation and a printed fallback list, with Contributor 03 supplying the policy correction. The implementation record alone does not prove desk use.

After Contributor 05 found a midnight date fault and supplied tests for both entry routes, I reproduced it, changed conversion to the desk date and tested the correction; both routes then preserved the entered date. The correction was tested on the desk's two documented date-entry routes, not broader environments.

I treated the two exceptions as evidence that a form alone did not resolve policy ambiguity, then added a visible escalation note beside the approver field instead of another status label and kept the printed fallback aligned; Contributor 03 reviewed the wording. The note was implemented, but independent volunteer use had not been tested.
decisions: I traced requests through three handoffs and chose to add next-owner and return-date fields to the existing shared form instead of introducing a new application, because volunteers used a shared computer and another login would add a step. The shared-computer constraint is my contemporaneous report; this does not establish that it was the only possible design.

My first draft wrongly combined owner and approver; after Contributor 03 explained the policy boundary, I separated the fields and acknowledged that I should have checked it before drafting. Contributor 03 supplied the policy correction; I made the implementation change.
I offered to add return reminders if response ownership was agreed, but I had not built them. This was an offer with a dependency, not an executed feature.
accounts.sharedCredit: Contributor 04 ran the first North Desk shift and owned daily review while I handled defects; the printed fallback stayed available for the shared-computer queue. This establishes the operational handoff and first-shift use, not independent volunteer operation.
accounts.outcome:
Across two supervised shifts run by Contributor 04 and observed by Contributor 06, seven of nine return requests had a named next owner before handoff; the other two needed coordinator help. There was no baseline or turnaround-time measure, and the raw-row attachment was unavailable.
